items.summaryZh: 本研究摘要指出，英国与荷兰在农业食品和农业科技领域开展人工智能合作的机遇，将英国的研究与数字创新同荷兰在部署、规模化及粮食系统整合方面的优势相结合。
items.titleZh: 荷兰与英国的人工智能生态系统：农业食品与农业科技
zhParas: 研究摘要发布于2026年10月8日
图片由 Smart Future / Adobe Stock 提供
本简报重点介绍了关于英国—荷兰在农业食品和农业科技技术领域人工智能（AI）合作机会的主要发现，借鉴了兰德欧洲为外交、联邦和发展事务部（FCDO）对两国人工智能生态系统所作的评估。该报告由FCDO于2025年委托编写，旨在为两国国家人工智能生态系统的优势与挑战提供证据基础，并结合2025年英国—荷兰创新伙伴关系，探讨互补行动与协同的领域。

英国和荷兰都拥有强大的人工智能生态系统，且优势互补。英国提供规模、全球连接和研究深度，其科技产业价值约1万亿英镑，人工智能收入在2024年增长68%。[1] 科学、创新与技术部（DSIT）、英国研究与创新署（UKRI）和艾伦·图灵研究所等公共机构支撑着该生态系统，而与荷兰相比，初创企业还可受益于更雄厚的投资纵深以及更先进的超大规模和数据中心能力。荷兰的生态系统规模较小，但网络化程度很高，得到强有力的公私协调支持，并凭借半导体和使能技术优势在人工智能价值链中具有战略重要性。
两国在创新驱动型增长、负责任监管、算力与数据韧性以及技能发展方面有着相似的战略优先事项，同时也面临人才和基础设施方面的相似制约。通过“地平线欧洲”、七国集团和经合组织人工智能原则，以及2025年英国—荷兰创新伙伴关系开展的现有合作，意味着两国双边合作已经具备一致的基础。
本简报是一项更广泛分析的一部分，该分析围绕英国—荷兰人工智能生态系统的三个优先领域展开：
面向人工智能的计算，
生命科学与健康技术，以及
农业食品与农业科技。
选择这些领域，是因为它们体现了不同但互补的双边机遇形式，并能在两国展示出雄厚的产业基础和政策优先地位。计算是更广泛人工智能能力与韧性的基础性赋能要素；生命科学与健康技术是共同的战略优势领域，两国在研究、创新和政策上高度一致；农业食品与农业科技则是一个优势互补的领域，将荷兰的应用引领地位与英国在研发和数字创新方面的优势相结合。
农业食品与农业科技是英国和荷兰人工智能生态系统中的战略优势领域。虽然两国都认识到人工智能是粮食系统生产力、可持续性和韧性的关键赋能要素，但荷兰展现出更成熟、更一体化的农业食品人工智能生态系统，而英国则贡献了强大的上游研究、数字创新和使能技术。
专利和投资证据凸显了荷兰在应用型农业人工智能领域的领先地位。荷兰在农业和食品相关分类中的专利活动高于英国，反映出其在园艺和智能农业机械等领域拥有更先进的商业化管线。英国农业食品与农业科技生态系统的规模较小，但在研究、试验和数字创新方面展现出显著优势。
在这两个国家，AI被视为对紧迫结构性压力的应对之策，而非渐进式优化。这些压力包括劳动力短缺、气候波动、化肥和用水限制以及能源成本上升。尽管创新活动强劲，但两个生态系统中农民和生产者对AI的采用仍不均衡，尤其是在较小的农业企业中。采用的障碍包括数据系统碎片化、数据所有权和责任归属的不确定性、数字技能参差不齐，以及对AI赋能的决策支持工具信任有限。
综合来看，这些动态为双边合作奠定了坚实基础。荷兰提供可部署环境、系统集成和规模化能力，而英国提供上游创新、灵活试验和数字能力。将英国研发与荷兰的应用、验证和市场路径相衔接的协调行动，明确有潜力加速两国农业食品系统对AI的采用，同时支持可持续性、生产力和食品系统韧性方面的共同目标。
农业食品和农业科技在两国均具有战略优先地位，但在国家AI议程中占据不同位置。在荷兰，农业食品通过行业特定战略被嵌入为核心AI应用领域。荷兰政策强调将AI赋能的农业食品和农业科技发展作为全系统转型目标，反映出该部门在经济中的核心作用。在英国，农业科技在更横向的AI战略中被定位为前沿创新领域。政策工具侧重于激励创新、生产率增长和环境韧性，但不具备荷兰那样的部门中心性。
两国面临相似的结构性压力，这些压力提升了AI在农业食品领域的政策相关性，包括劳动力短缺、气候波动、投入品短缺和可持续性约束。然而，政策路径的侧重点存在分歧：荷兰战略强调协调一致的系统转型和部署准备，而英国政策更重视上游研发、试验和使能技术。
共同压力为合作提供了强有力理由，但政策框架的差异意味着，双边倡议在将荷兰在部署和系统集成方面的优势与英国在上游创新和灵活试验方面的优势相结合时最为有效。

荷兰在AI赋能的农业食品和农业科技领域拥有产业领先地位，其基础是规模、一体化和出口导向。荷兰农业食品部门约占国民经济和就业的10%，2025年农业食品技术的风险资本投资达到约7.3亿美元，使其成为该国最重要的投资领域之一。专利分析显示，荷兰在与农业和食品相关的国际专利分类（IPC）类别中活动强劲，反映出更成熟的商业化路径。产业领导力集中在园艺、受控环境农业、农业机器人和智能机械等领域，并得到具有全球竞争力的企业和密集供应链整合的支撑。
英国农业科技产业规模较小，但展现出较强的创新能力和细分领域专业化。2025年，英国农业科技投资达到约5.75亿美元，并得到由初创企业、研究机构和试验平台组成的分散式生态系统的支持。行业活动聚焦于农业机器人、传感技术、气候监测、生物技术以及人工智能赋能的质量控制。然而，有证据表明，商业采用仍不均衡，许多创新停滞在试点或早期部署阶段。
在两个生态系统中，采用情况仍不均衡，尤其是在小型生产者中。尽管技术潜力已得到验证，但障碍包括资金约束、数据系统碎片化、数据所有权的不确定性以及对人工智能工具的信任有限。
英国提供了强大的早期创新和专业技术储备，而荷兰提供了经过验证的部署和规模化路径。联合倡议可以通过整合互补的产业优势，降低商业化风险并加快采用。
- 开发联合试点，将英国技术与荷兰种植者、生产者和农业食品平台配对。此外，一个互补方向可以支持反向交流，使英国农民、企业和政策制定者能够直接学习荷兰在采用、整合和规模化方面的做法。由行业主导的试点可以依托现有的实验农场、商业场地和温室基础设施，并将早期创新锚定在真实运营环境中，帮助弥合研发与大规模部署之间的差距。
- 利用双边商业网络和现有联系，识别市场进入和规模化机会。现有的创新生态系统，如瓦赫宁根食品谷和英国农业科技集群，可以作为合作、投资和部署的切入点。这些网络还可以促进商业伙伴、技术开发者和最终用户之间的联系，减少采用障碍。
- 围绕机器人、精准农业、受控环境农业和供应链优化等实际用例建立伙伴关系。以实际应用为基础的伙伴关系能创造从创新到实施的更清晰路径。通过聚焦优先领域，利益相关方可以汇集资源和专业知识，在农业食品系统中提供可规模化、高影响力的解决方案。
关于协调基因编辑和精准育种规则的双边对话。监管对齐有助于建立长期趋同和实质性协调的路径，并提供一条减少碎片化、为创新建立更清晰、更一致框架的途径。这将使跨司法辖区运营的开发者和生产者受益，同时支持更顺畅的市场准入和供应链整合。这还将提高基因编辑技术及其产品的商业化潜力，因为它们将能够面向大得多的市场。

英国和荷兰都在人工智能赋能的农业食品和农业科技创新的研究基础方面表现强劲，但特点各异。荷兰受益于高度集中且全球公认的研究集群，尤其是瓦赫宁根大学与研究中心和瓦赫宁根食品谷，它们将人工智能研究与农业应用科学、产业合作和现实世界部署相结合。由荷兰研究理事会（NWO）和荷兰国家人工智能创新中心（ICAI）协调的国家研究计划，进一步强化了这种以可持续性、生产力和系统优化为重点的应用型、使命驱动型研究模式。
英国的研究格局更广泛但更分散，涵盖大学、专门的农业科技研究所以及应用中心，如洛桑研究所、Fera Science和英国农业科技中心。英国的优势尤其体现在上游人工智能研究、数据科学、建模、传感技术和早期实验方面，但通常与大规模农业部署环境的联系较弱。
科学计量学和定性证据表明，双边研究合作确实存在，但在农业食品领域相比生命科学仍不够发达。合作往往是基于项目的，并通过欧洲或多边框架促成，而不是通过持续的双边计划进行。
荷兰高度一体化的从研究到部署的路径，与英国在农业食品和农业科技发现层面研究的优势形成互补。结构化交流、共享测试平台和联合试点，可以大幅提升两国农业食品人工智能研究的转化影响。

- 联合研究能力，以建立人工智能农业食品生活实验室，在运营环境中测试精准喷洒、自动监测、温室优化和决策支持工具等技术。生活实验室具有明显优势：能够促进开发者与最终用户之间的协同设计，确保解决方案实用、以用户为中心并更容易被采用。这有助于及早发现特定情境下的挑战，并通过利益相关者的认可加速规模化。作为务实的第一步，这些举措可以依托两国现有基础设施和网络，例如试验农场、温室设施和成熟创新集群，从而降低启动成本并加快实施。然而，协调这些举措也可能耗费大量资源，并可能面临治理、数据共享以及协调不同参与者激励措施方面的挑战。
组建跨境联合体以参与“地平线欧洲”项目，尤其是在英国企业提供人工智能工具或传感技术、而荷兰合作伙伴提供已具备部署条件的环境和供应链整合的情况下。
- 扩大在基因编辑和精准育种方面的联合研发项目。在基因编辑领域加强合作可带来重要科学效益，但近期进展需要资金安排和审批途径。实践中，最可行的合作形式很可能是有针对性的学术交流、联合研讨会和竞争前研究试点。
- 双边农业数据互操作性框架。共同原则和技术标准有助于确保两国的农业数据集能够在研究、咨询和商业环境中更可靠地使用。初步重点领域可包括通用元数据标准、共享的作物和土壤数据本体，以及更清晰的数据访问和使用规则，以支持跨境合作与创新。
以下机遇主要涉及这样一些领域：政策和制度支持可以加强两国研究人员、企业、农民及其他农食领域参与者之间合作的条件。其中一些机遇，例如生活实验室和“地平线欧洲”联合投标，在短期内也与外部利益相关者直接相关。另一些机遇，尤其是与农业数据互操作性和基因相关的机遇，则更可能取决于协调一致的政策行动、技术对接，以及在某些情况下较长期的监管。

研究摘要发布于2026年10月8日

图片由 Smart Future / Adobe Stock 提供

本简报重点介绍了关于英国—荷兰在农业食品和农业科技技术领域人工智能（AI）合作机会的主要发现，借鉴了兰德欧洲为外交、联邦和发展事务部（FCDO）对两国人工智能生态系统所作的评估。该报告由FCDO于2025年委托编写，旨在为两国国家人工智能生态系统的优势与挑战提供证据基础，并结合2025年英国—荷兰创新伙伴关系，探讨互补行动与协同的领域。

英国和荷兰都拥有强大的人工智能生态系统，且优势互补。英国提供规模、全球连接和研究深度，其科技产业价值约1万亿英镑，人工智能收入在2024年增长68%。[1] 科学、创新与技术部（DSIT）、英国研究与创新署（UKRI）和艾伦·图灵研究所等公共机构支撑着该生态系统，而与荷兰相比，初创企业还可受益于更雄厚的投资纵深以及更先进的超大规模和数据中心能力。荷兰的生态系统规模较小，但网络化程度很高，得到强有力的公私协调支持，并凭借半导体和使能技术优势在人工智能价值链中具有战略重要性。

两国在创新驱动型增长、负责任监管、算力与数据韧性以及技能发展方面有着相似的战略优先事项，同时也面临人才和基础设施方面的相似制约。通过“地平线欧洲”、七国集团和经合组织人工智能原则，以及2025年英国—荷兰创新伙伴关系开展的现有合作，意味着两国双边合作已经具备一致的基础。

本简报是一项更广泛分析的一部分，该分析围绕英国—荷兰人工智能生态系统的三个优先领域展开：

面向人工智能的计算，

生命科学与健康技术，以及

农业食品与农业科技。

选择这些领域，是因为它们体现了不同但互补的双边机遇形式，并能在两国展示出雄厚的产业基础和政策优先地位。计算是更广泛人工智能能力与韧性的基础性赋能要素；生命科学与健康技术是共同的战略优势领域，两国在研究、创新和政策上高度一致；农业食品与农业科技则是一个优势互补的领域，将荷兰的应用引领地位与英国在研发和数字创新方面的优势相结合。

农业食品与农业科技是英国和荷兰人工智能生态系统中的战略优势领域。虽然两国都认识到人工智能是粮食系统生产力、可持续性和韧性的关键赋能要素，但荷兰展现出更成熟、更一体化的农业食品人工智能生态系统，而英国则贡献了强大的上游研究、数字创新和使能技术。

专利和投资证据凸显了荷兰在应用型农业人工智能领域的领先地位。荷兰在农业和食品相关分类中的专利活动高于英国，反映出其在园艺和智能农业机械等领域拥有更先进的商业化管线。英国农业食品与农业科技生态系统的规模较小，但在研究、试验和数字创新方面展现出显著优势。

在这两个国家，AI被视为对紧迫结构性压力的应对之策，而非渐进式优化。这些压力包括劳动力短缺、气候波动、化肥和用水限制以及能源成本上升。尽管创新活动强劲，但两个生态系统中农民和生产者对AI的采用仍不均衡，尤其是在较小的农业企业中。采用的障碍包括数据系统碎片化、数据所有权和责任归属的不确定性、数字技能参差不齐，以及对AI赋能的决策支持工具信任有限。

综合来看，这些动态为双边合作奠定了坚实基础。荷兰提供可部署环境、系统集成和规模化能力，而英国提供上游创新、灵活试验和数字能力。将英国研发与荷兰的应用、验证和市场路径相衔接的协调行动，明确有潜力加速两国农业食品系统对AI的采用，同时支持可持续性、生产力和食品系统韧性方面的共同目标。

农业食品和农业科技在两国均具有战略优先地位，但在国家AI议程中占据不同位置。在荷兰，农业食品通过行业特定战略被嵌入为核心AI应用领域。荷兰政策强调将AI赋能的农业食品和农业科技发展作为全系统转型目标，反映出该部门在经济中的核心作用。在英国，农业科技在更横向的AI战略中被定位为前沿创新领域。政策工具侧重于激励创新、生产率增长和环境韧性，但不具备荷兰那样的部门中心性。

两国面临相似的结构性压力，这些压力提升了AI在农业食品领域的政策相关性，包括劳动力短缺、气候波动、投入品短缺和可持续性约束。然而，政策路径的侧重点存在分歧：荷兰战略强调协调一致的系统转型和部署准备，而英国政策更重视上游研发、试验和使能技术。

共同压力为合作提供了强有力理由，但政策框架的差异意味着，双边倡议在将荷兰在部署和系统集成方面的优势与英国在上游创新和灵活试验方面的优势相结合时最为有效。

荷兰在AI赋能的农业食品和农业科技领域拥有产业领先地位，其基础是规模、一体化和出口导向。荷兰农业食品部门约占国民经济和就业的10%，2025年农业食品技术的风险资本投资达到约7.3亿美元，使其成为该国最重要的投资领域之一。专利分析显示，荷兰在与农业和食品相关的国际专利分类（IPC）类别中活动强劲，反映出更成熟的商业化路径。产业领导力集中在园艺、受控环境农业、农业机器人和智能机械等领域，并得到具有全球竞争力的企业和密集供应链整合的支撑。

英国农业科技产业规模较小，但展现出较强的创新能力和细分领域专业化。2025年，英国农业科技投资达到约5.75亿美元，并得到由初创企业、研究机构和试验平台组成的分散式生态系统的支持。行业活动聚焦于农业机器人、传感技术、气候监测、生物技术以及人工智能赋能的质量控制。然而，有证据表明，商业采用仍不均衡，许多创新停滞在试点或早期部署阶段。

在两个生态系统中，采用情况仍不均衡，尤其是在小型生产者中。尽管技术潜力已得到验证，但障碍包括资金约束、数据系统碎片化、数据所有权的不确定性以及对人工智能工具的信任有限。

英国提供了强大的早期创新和专业技术储备，而荷兰提供了经过验证的部署和规模化路径。联合倡议可以通过整合互补的产业优势，降低商业化风险并加快采用。

- 开发联合试点，将英国技术与荷兰种植者、生产者和农业食品平台配对。此外，一个互补方向可以支持反向交流，使英国农民、企业和政策制定者能够直接学习荷兰在采用、整合和规模化方面的做法。由行业主导的试点可以依托现有的实验农场、商业场地和温室基础设施，并将早期创新锚定在真实运营环境中，帮助弥合研发与大规模部署之间的差距。

- 利用双边商业网络和现有联系，识别市场进入和规模化机会。现有的创新生态系统，如瓦赫宁根食品谷和英国农业科技集群，可以作为合作、投资和部署的切入点。这些网络还可以促进商业伙伴、技术开发者和最终用户之间的联系，减少采用障碍。

- 围绕机器人、精准农业、受控环境农业和供应链优化等实际用例建立伙伴关系。以实际应用为基础的伙伴关系能创造从创新到实施的更清晰路径。通过聚焦优先领域，利益相关方可以汇集资源和专业知识，在农业食品系统中提供可规模化、高影响力的解决方案。

关于协调基因编辑和精准育种规则的双边对话。监管对齐有助于建立长期趋同和实质性协调的路径，并提供一条减少碎片化、为创新建立更清晰、更一致框架的途径。这将使跨司法辖区运营的开发者和生产者受益，同时支持更顺畅的市场准入和供应链整合。这还将提高基因编辑技术及其产品的商业化潜力，因为它们将能够面向大得多的市场。

英国和荷兰都在人工智能赋能的农业食品和农业科技创新的研究基础方面表现强劲，但特点各异。荷兰受益于高度集中且全球公认的研究集群，尤其是瓦赫宁根大学与研究中心和瓦赫宁根食品谷，它们将人工智能研究与农业应用科学、产业合作和现实世界部署相结合。由荷兰研究理事会（NWO）和荷兰国家人工智能创新中心（ICAI）协调的国家研究计划，进一步强化了这种以可持续性、生产力和系统优化为重点的应用型、使命驱动型研究模式。

英国的研究格局更广泛但更分散，涵盖大学、专门的农业科技研究所以及应用中心，如洛桑研究所、Fera Science和英国农业科技中心。英国的优势尤其体现在上游人工智能研究、数据科学、建模、传感技术和早期实验方面，但通常与大规模农业部署环境的联系较弱。

科学计量学和定性证据表明，双边研究合作确实存在，但在农业食品领域相比生命科学仍不够发达。合作往往是基于项目的，并通过欧洲或多边框架促成，而不是通过持续的双边计划进行。

荷兰高度一体化的从研究到部署的路径，与英国在农业食品和农业科技发现层面研究的优势形成互补。结构化交流、共享测试平台和联合试点，可以大幅提升两国农业食品人工智能研究的转化影响。

- 扩大在基因编辑和精准育种方面的联合研发项目。在基因编辑领域加强合作可带来重要科学效益，但近期进展需要资金安排和审批途径。实践中，最可行的合作形式很可能是有针对性的学术交流、联合研讨会和竞争前研究试点。

Research SummaryPublished Oct 8, 2026

This research was sponsored by UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)

Photo by putilov_denis / Adobe Stock

This briefing highlights key findings on opportunities for UK–Netherlands collaboration with compute for artificial intelligence (AI) for the life sciences and health technologies, drawing on RAND Europe’s assessment for the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) of AI ecosystems in both countries. The report was commissioned by FCDO in 2025 to provide an evidence base on the strengths and challenges in both countries’ national AI ecosystems, as well as to explore areas for complementary action and synergy in light of the 2025 UK–Netherlands Innovation Partnership.

The UK and the Netherlands are both strong AI ecosystems with complementary strengths. The UK offers scale, global connectivity and research depth, with a tech sector worth around £1 trillion and AI revenues growing by 68% in 2024.[1] Public institutions such as the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) and the Alan Turing Institute anchor the ecosystem, while start-ups can benefit from greater investment depth and a more advanced hyperscale and data centre capacity compared to the Netherlands. The Netherlands has a smaller but highly networked ecosystem supported by strong public-private coordination and strategic importance in AI value chains through semiconductor and enabling technology strengths.

Both countries share similar strategic priorities around innovation-led growth, responsible regulation, compute and data resilience, and skills development, while also facing similar constraints in talent and infrastructure. Existing cooperation through Horizon Europe, the G7 and the OECD AI Principles, alongside the 2025 UK–Netherlands Innovation Partnership, mean there is already a coherent foundation for bilateral cooperation between the two countries.

This briefing is part of a wider analysis organised around three priority sectors for UK–Netherlands AI ecosystems: (1) compute for AI, (2) life sciences and health technologies and (3) agrifood and agritech. These sectors were selected because they capture different but complementary forms of bilateral opportunity and can demonstrate a strong industrial foundation and policy prioritisation in both countries. Compute functions as a foundational enabler of wider AI capability and resilience; life sciences and health technologies represent an area of shared strategic strength, with strong research, innovation and policy alignment in both countries; and agrifood and agritech represents a domain of complementary advantage, combining Dutch applied leadership with UK strengths in R&D and digital innovation.

Compute capacity is a strategic enabler of AI leadership, economic resilience and national security. Both the UK and the Netherlands treat compute as critical infrastructure underpinning productivity, innovation and sovereign AI capability. Policy choices on compute now shape who can train, deploy and govern advanced AI systems in the next decade.

The UK's approach prioritises national scale and speed. This involves direct public investment in AI-dedicated supercomputers, accelerated data centre planning and strong partnerships with global hyperscalers. The Netherlands pursues strategic relevance through integration, embedding national capability within EU-level compute, cloud and research infrastructures.

The distinction is not ambition but governance. UK policy emphasises domestic control and rapid capacity expansion; Dutch policy emphasises interoperability, coordination and shared European assets.

In the UK, policy has unlocked large-scale public and private investment. Government has committed multi-billion-pound funding to expand AI compute twentyfold by 2030, established central coordinating bodies (including a sovereign AI unit) and attracted major hyperscaler and data centre investments. This has reinforced the UK's position as a leading European hub for AI-optimised compute infrastructure while stimulating innovation in hardware design, cooling and modular data centre systems. However, rapid expansion has also exposed fragmentation, oversubscription of public compute, grid bottlenecks and skills shortages.

The Netherlands has focused on coordinated provision rather than scale. Public funding through AINed, SURF and the AI Coalition for the Netherlands (AIC4NL) supports shared access to compute, strong integration of high-performance computing (HPC) and cloud, and participation in EuroHPC. Dutch strengths lie in world-class digital connectivity, energy-efficient infrastructure and system integration. Structural constraints—limited grid capacity, land-use restrictions, funding gaps and weaker growth-stage finance—cap near-term expansion and increase reliance on EU-level assets. Both countries face acute shortages in AI, compute and energy-system skills.

Both countries are investing to support AI model training and deployment but follow different paths. The UK is building frontier-scale national systems alongside commercial cloud capacity, positioning itself as a location for training and running large models. The Netherlands relies more heavily on EU-scale supercomputing and federated access, accepting that frontier compute will be shared rather than nationally owned.

Despite these differences, both remain heavily dependent on US hyperscalers, which control the majority of available AI compute. Shared constraints are acute: grid congestion, long connection timelines, rising energy costs, planning restrictions and environmental pressures. Data centre location choices are increasingly constrained by energy availability rather than demand. These factors risk slowing AI deployment, increasing costs, and deepening dependence on foreign infrastructure.

The UK and the Netherlands face common strategic challenges including insufficient compute at scale, energy and grid constraints, skills shortages and reliance on non-European providers. These shared pressures create clear opportunities for bilateral cooperation. Priority areas include aligning standards for sustainable data centres; coordinating access to high-end compute; joint approaches to talent development; and exploring cross-border, energy-linked compute solutions, particularly in the North Sea. Cooperation would strengthen resilience, reduce duplication and reinforce Europe's strategic position in AI.

UK and Dutch compute policies are aligned in intent but diverge in execution. In the UK, the National AI Strategy, Modern Industrial Strategy, and Digital and Technologies Sector Plan highlight data and compute resources as foundational to AI leadership and critical enablers of productivity nationwide. The UK Compute Roadmap commits £2bn by 2030 to a 'modern public compute ecosystem' largely geared towards AI. Overall, the UK treats compute as a sovereign capability and growth lever, deploying significant public capital, central coordination and planning reform to accelerate capacity. The Netherlands embeds compute within EU frameworks, prioritising interoperability, shared infrastructure and strategic relevance over national ownership. EU legislation such as the Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) is bolstering the diffusion of AI and the adoption of cloud across the Netherlands through Europe-wide efforts. At the same time, national efforts such as the Strategic Action Plan for AI highlights the importance of compute and data resources alongside skills and research for developing the Dutch AI economy.

Both approaches face constraints. In the UK, fragmentation across public, academic and commercial compute, oversubscription of national resources, grid delays and skills shortages risk limiting returns on investment. In the Netherlands, constrained funding, land-use restrictions, grid saturation and limited access to frontierscale compute restrict scalability. Both ecosystems remain exposed to dependence on US hyperscalers.

These differences matter because they are complementary. UK scale and capital mobilisation combine well with Dutch strengths in coordination, connectivity and EU integration. A more deliberate alignment—on standards, access models, sustainability and talent—could deliver greater collective resilience than either approach alone.

Private investment is driving compute expansion in both countries, but at different scales. The UK has attracted exceptionally large hyperscaler and data centre commitments, reinforcing its role as a European AI compute hub and supporting a growing ecosystem of specialist suppliers. The Netherlands continues to attract investment from major players, enabled by connectivity and sustainability credentials, but expansion is constrained by zoning and grid limits. Industry faces shared barriers including high and volatile energy costs, grid access delays, land scarcity, skills shortages and lock-in to proprietary cloud ecosystems. These factors raise costs, slow deployment and limit the emergence of competitive European alternatives.

Shared barriers also mean that future competitiveness is increasingly dependent on the interlinkage of infrastructure development and factors such as permitting, energy prices, grid access and connectivity. Additionally, cross-border AI development is constrained not only by compute access but also by data sensitivity and sovereignty concerns, which might limit how firms collaborate.

Bilateral cooperation could improve industry outcomes by enabling pooled procurement, shared standards for green data centres, joint testing environments and coordinated engagement with hyperscalers. This would strengthen negotiating leverage, reduce duplication and support a more resilient European compute supply chain. Over the longer term it could also support more coordinated approaches to sustainable compute infrastructure.

- Explore collaboration on privacy-preserving model development, where cross-border AI development is limited by data regulatory or sovereignty concerns. In these cases, federated learning is a promising route for joint work without requiring raw data to be shared across jurisdictions.

- Use bilateral engagement to better understand complementary infrastructure environments. Firms can benefit from learning how UK scale and Dutch coordination create different advantages in deployment, connectivity and infrastructure use.

- Shared work on sustainable compute and energy integration is a promising opportunity, but would require stronger policy and institutional support to move beyond dialogue into coordinated action. At the level of policy, a bilateral compute treaty could facilitate a coordinated approach to tackling challenges to sovereign compute such as energy access, data access, sustainability, and the spatial distribution of data centre capacity.

- More structured coordination on standards, access models and resilience could benefit industry, although these are primarily areas for future bilateral strategy and policy development. One option would be a bilateral compute strategy that aligns approaches to sovereign compute, infrastructure resilience and sustainable expansion.

The UK research landscape is highly concentrated. Elite universities command significant compute resources and attract major investment, but oversubscription and fragmentation limit access for smaller institutions. This risks slowing experimentation and widening gaps between research leaders and the wider system.

The Netherlands operates a more integrated model through SURF, providing broad access to HPC and cloud resources and strong links to EU-level compute. However, national capacity is insufficient for frontierscale model training and chronic funding constraints limit expansion. Talent retention is also a challenge.

Across both countries, academia faces common barriers including limited access to cutting-edge GPUs, rising compute costs, skills shortages in research support roles and regulatory friction around data sharing. As mentioned above, barriers to cross-border collaboration include not only infrastructure but also the inability to work on sensitive datasets across institutional or country boundaries. This underlines the usefulness of privacy-preserving approaches for joint model development and training.

Closer UK–Netherlands cooperation could expand effective access to compute, support joint training and mobility schemes, and improve utilisation of European supercomputing assets. This would enhance research competitiveness, support innovation diffusion and strengthen the UK–Netherlands' contribution to the European AI research base.

- Explore privacy-preserving approaches to joint model training and development where cross-border collaboration is constrained by data sensitivity. Federated learning is one pragmatic route for collaboration without requiring data sharing.

- Use existing European infrastructures and relationships where possible. The UK's renewed connection to EuroHPC improves the basis for researchers to deepen collaboration with Dutch and wider European compute actors.

- Shared training, fellowships and researcher mobility schemes are identified as a significant opportunity but would require policy and institutional backing to be implemented at scale. Now that the UK has rejoined the EuroHPC ecosystem, joint upskilling programmes could be leveraged to tackle skill gaps and promote the exchange of expertise across supercompute clusters. Similarly, joint participation in instruments such as Marie Skłodowska-Curie fellowships and Erasmus+ Knowledge Alliances could permit development of cross-border educational programmes in advanced computing.

- Closer alignment around compute access and the use of shared infrastructure would also require institutional coordination beyond what individual researchers can establish alone.

The opportunities below are primarily areas where policy and institutional support could strengthen the conditions for collaboration between researchers, firms and innovation actors in both countries. Some, such as exchanges, networking and joint training, are also directly relevant to external stakeholders in the near term. Others, particularly those related to compute access, infrastructure coordination and standards, are more likely to depend on coordinated policy action and longer-term institutional alignment.

items.summaryZh: 该研究摘要指出了英国与荷兰在生命科学和健康领域开展人工智能合作的机会，将英国的商业规模和研究深度与荷兰的临床整合、验证及欧洲市场路径相连接。
items.titleZh: 荷兰与英国的人工智能生态系统：人工智能算力
zhParas: 研究摘要发布于2026年10月8日
本研究由英国外交、联邦和发展事务部（FCDO）资助
图片：putilov_denis / Adobe Stock
本简报重点介绍了英国与荷兰在生命科学和健康技术领域围绕人工智能（AI）算力开展合作机会的主要发现，借鉴了兰德欧洲为英国外交、联邦和发展事务部（FCDO）对两国人工智能生态系统所作的评估。该报告由FCDO于2025年委托编写，旨在为两国国家人工智能生态系统的优势与挑战提供证据基础，并根据2025年英国—荷兰创新伙伴关系探索互补行动与协同领域。

英国和荷兰都拥有强大的人工智能生态系统，且优势互补。英国具备规模、全球连通性和研究深度，其科技行业价值约1万亿英镑，2024年人工智能收入增长68%。[1] 科学、创新与技术部（DSIT）、英国研究与创新署（UKRI）和艾伦·图灵研究所等公共机构构成生态系统的支柱，而与荷兰相比，初创企业可受益于更雄厚的投资深度以及更先进的超大规模和数据中心能力。荷兰的生态系统规模较小，但网络化程度很高，得到强有力的公私协调支持，并凭借半导体和使能技术优势在人工智能价值链中具有战略重要性。
两国在创新驱动增长、负责任监管、算力与数据韧性以及技能发展方面有着相似的战略优先事项，同时也面临相似的人才和基础设施制约。通过“地平线欧洲”、七国集团和经合组织人工智能原则，以及2025年英国—荷兰创新伙伴关系开展的现有合作，意味着两国之间已经具备连贯的双边合作基础。

本简报是一项更广泛分析的一部分，该分析围绕英荷人工智能生态系统的三个优先领域展开：（1）人工智能算力，（2）生命科学与健康技术，（3）农业食品与农业科技。之所以选择这些领域，是因为它们体现了不同但互补的双边机遇形式，并能在两国展示出强大的产业基础和政策优先事项。算力是更广泛人工智能能力与韧性的基础性使能因素；生命科学与健康技术是双方共同战略优势的领域，两国在研究、创新和政策上高度一致；农业食品与农业科技则是一个优势互补的领域，将荷兰的应用引领与英国在研发和数字创新方面的优势结合起来。
算力容量是人工智能领导地位、经济韧性和国家安全的战略使能因素。英国和荷兰都将算力视为支撑生产力、创新和主权人工智能能力的关键基础设施。如今在算力方面的政策选择，将决定未来十年谁能够训练、部署和治理先进人工智能系统。
英国的做法优先考虑国家规模与速度。这包括对专用于人工智能的超级计算机进行直接公共投资、加快数据中心规划审批，以及与全球超大规模云服务商建立牢固伙伴关系。荷兰则通过一体化追求战略相关性，将国家能力嵌入欧盟层面的算力、云和研究基础设施之中。
区别不在于雄心，而在于治理。英国政策强调国内控制和快速扩张算力；荷兰政策强调互操作性、协调以及共享的欧洲资产。
在英国，政策释放了大规模公共和私人投资。政府已承诺投入数十亿英镑资金，到2030年将人工智能算力扩大二十倍，设立了中央协调机构（包括一个主权人工智能部门），并吸引了超大规模云服务商和数据中心的大型投资。这巩固了英国作为欧洲领先的人工智能优化算力基础设施枢纽的地位，同时促进了硬件设计、冷却和模块化数据中心系统方面的创新。然而，快速扩张也暴露出碎片化、公共算力超额认购、电网瓶颈和技能短缺等问题。

荷兰侧重于协调供给而非规模。通过 AINed、SURF 和荷兰人工智能联盟（AIC4NL）提供的公共资金，支持算力共享访问、高性能计算（HPC）与云的有力整合，以及参与 EuroHPC。荷兰的优势在于世界一流的数字连接、节能基础设施和系统集成。结构性制约——电网容量有限、土地使用限制、资金缺口以及成长阶段融资较弱——限制了近期扩张，并增加了对欧盟层面资产的依赖。两国都面临人工智能、算力和能源系统技能方面的严重短缺。
两国都在投资以支持人工智能模型的训练和部署，但所走路径不同。英国正在建设前沿规模的国家系统，并配套商业云能力，将自身定位为训练和运行大型模型的地点。荷兰则更依赖欧盟规模的超算和联邦式访问，接受前沿算力将共享而非国家所有。
尽管存在这些差异，两国仍严重依赖美国超大规模云服务商，后者控制着可用人工智能算力的多数。共同制约十分严峻：电网拥堵、并网周期漫长、能源成本上升、规划限制和环境压力。数据中心选址日益受制于能源可获得性，而非需求。这些因素可能导致人工智能部署放缓、成本上升，并加深对外国基础设施的依赖。
英国和荷兰面临共同的战略挑战，包括规模化算力不足、能源和电网制约、技能短缺以及对非欧洲供应商的依赖。这些共同压力为双边合作创造了明确机遇。优先领域包括：统一可持续数据中心标准；协调高端算力获取；在人才发展上采取联合方式；以及探索跨境、与能源相联的算力解决方案，尤其是在北海。合作将增强韧性、减少重复建设，并巩固欧洲在人工智能领域的战略地位。

英国和荷兰的算力政策在意图上一致，但在执行上存在分歧。在英国，《国家人工智能战略》《现代工业战略》和《数字与技术行业计划》都将数据和算力资源列为人工智能领导地位的基础，以及全国生产力的关键使能因素。英国《算力路线图》承诺到2030年投入20亿英镑，建设一个“现代公共算力生态系统”，主要面向人工智能。总体而言，英国将算力视为主权能力和增长杠杆，投入大量公共资本，进行中央协调并推动规划改革，以加速算力建设。荷兰则将算力嵌入欧盟框架，优先考虑互操作性、共享基础设施和战略相关性，而非国家所有。欧盟立法，如《云与人工智能发展法案》（CADA），正通过全欧洲的努力，推动人工智能在荷兰的普及和云的采用。与此同时，荷兰的国家努力，如《人工智能战略行动计划》，强调算力和数据资源与技能、研究一样，对发展荷兰人工智能经济至关重要。
两种路径都面临制约。在英国，公共、学术和商业算力之间彼此割裂，国家资源超额认购，电网延迟和技能短缺，可能限制投资回报。在荷兰，资金受限、土地使用限制、电网饱和以及获取前沿规模算力的渠道有限，制约了可扩展性。两个生态系统都仍然面临依赖美国超大规模云服务商的风险。
这些差异之所以重要，是因为它们具有互补性。英国的规模和资本调动能力，与荷兰在协调、互联互通和欧盟一体化方面的优势相结合，能够形成良好互补。在标准、访问模式、可持续性和人才方面进行更有意识的协调，可能比任一单独路径带来更强的集体韧性。

私人投资正在推动两国的算力扩张，但规模不同。英国已吸引异常庞大的超大规模云服务商和数据中心承诺，巩固其作为欧洲人工智能算力枢纽的角色，并支撑不断壮大的专业供应商生态系统。荷兰继续吸引主要参与者的投资，这得益于其连通性和可持续性资质，但扩张受到分区规划和电网限制的制约。行业面临共同障碍，包括高昂且波动的能源成本、电网接入延迟、土地稀缺、技能短缺以及对专有云生态系统的锁定。这些因素推高成本、减缓部署，并限制有竞争力的欧洲替代方案出现。
共同障碍还意味着，未来的竞争力越来越依赖于基础设施发展同许可审批、能源价格、电网接入和连通性等因素之间的相互关联。此外，跨境人工智能发展不仅受到算力获取的制约，还受到数据敏感性和主权关切的制约，这可能会限制企业合作的方式。
双边合作可以通过促成联合采购、绿色数据中心共同标准、联合测试环境以及与超大规模云服务商协调互动，改善行业成果。这将增强谈判筹码、减少重复建设，并支撑更具韧性的欧洲算力供应链。从更长期看，它还可以支持以更协调的方式推进可持续算力基础设施。
- 探索在隐私保护模型开发方面的合作，因为跨境人工智能开发受到数据监管或主权关切的限制。在这些情况下，联邦学习是一条有前景的路径，可在不要求原始数据跨司法辖区共享的情况下开展联合工作。
- 利用双边接触更好地理解互补的基础设施环境。企业可以通过了解英国的规模与荷兰的协调如何分别在部署、连通性和基础设施使用方面创造不同优势而受益。
- 在可持续算力和能源整合方面开展共同工作是很有前景的机遇，但需要更强的政策和制度支持，才能超越对话、进入协调行动。在政策层面，一项双边算力条约可以促进以协调方式应对主权算力面临的挑战，例如能源获取、数据获取、可持续性以及数据中心容量的空间分布。
在标准、接入模式和韧性方面进行更有条理的协调可能有利于产业，不过这些主要是未来战略与政策制定的领域。一个选项是制定双边算力战略，协调主权算力、基础设施韧性和可持续扩展方面的做法。
英国的研究格局高度集中。精英大学掌握大量算力资源并吸引重大投资，但供过于求和碎片化限制了规模较小机构的获取。这可能减缓试验探索，并拉大研究领军者与更广泛体系之间的差距。
荷兰通过SURF运行一种更一体化的模式，为高性能计算和云资源提供广泛接入，并与欧盟层面的算力紧密相连。然而，国家能力不足以进行前沿规模模型训练，长期资金制约限制了扩展。人才留存也是一项挑战。

在数据敏感性制约跨境合作的情况下，探索用于联合模型训练与开发的隐私保护方法。联邦学习是一条务实的合作路径，无需共享数据。

以下机遇主要是政策和制度支持能够加强两国研究人员、企业和创新主体之间合作条件的领域。其中一些，如交流、联络和联合培训，短期内也与外部利益相关方直接相关。另一些，特别是与算力获取、基础设施协调和标准相关的机遇，更可能取决于协调一致的政策行动和更长期的机构协同。

研究摘要发布于2026年10月8日

本研究由英国外交、联邦和发展事务部（FCDO）资助

图片：putilov_denis / Adobe Stock

本简报重点介绍了英国与荷兰在生命科学和健康技术领域围绕人工智能（AI）算力开展合作机会的主要发现，借鉴了兰德欧洲为英国外交、联邦和发展事务部（FCDO）对两国人工智能生态系统所作的评估。该报告由FCDO于2025年委托编写，旨在为两国国家人工智能生态系统的优势与挑战提供证据基础，并根据2025年英国—荷兰创新伙伴关系探索互补行动与协同领域。

英国和荷兰都拥有强大的人工智能生态系统，且优势互补。英国具备规模、全球连通性和研究深度，其科技行业价值约1万亿英镑，2024年人工智能收入增长68%。[1] 科学、创新与技术部（DSIT）、英国研究与创新署（UKRI）和艾伦·图灵研究所等公共机构构成生态系统的支柱，而与荷兰相比，初创企业可受益于更雄厚的投资深度以及更先进的超大规模和数据中心能力。荷兰的生态系统规模较小，但网络化程度很高，得到强有力的公私协调支持，并凭借半导体和使能技术优势在人工智能价值链中具有战略重要性。

两国在创新驱动增长、负责任监管、算力与数据韧性以及技能发展方面有着相似的战略优先事项，同时也面临相似的人才和基础设施制约。通过“地平线欧洲”、七国集团和经合组织人工智能原则，以及2025年英国—荷兰创新伙伴关系开展的现有合作，意味着两国之间已经具备连贯的双边合作基础。

本简报是一项更广泛分析的一部分，该分析围绕英荷人工智能生态系统的三个优先领域展开：（1）人工智能算力，（2）生命科学与健康技术，（3）农业食品与农业科技。之所以选择这些领域，是因为它们体现了不同但互补的双边机遇形式，并能在两国展示出强大的产业基础和政策优先事项。算力是更广泛人工智能能力与韧性的基础性使能因素；生命科学与健康技术是双方共同战略优势的领域，两国在研究、创新和政策上高度一致；农业食品与农业科技则是一个优势互补的领域，将荷兰的应用引领与英国在研发和数字创新方面的优势结合起来。

算力容量是人工智能领导地位、经济韧性和国家安全的战略使能因素。英国和荷兰都将算力视为支撑生产力、创新和主权人工智能能力的关键基础设施。如今在算力方面的政策选择，将决定未来十年谁能够训练、部署和治理先进人工智能系统。

英国的做法优先考虑国家规模与速度。这包括对专用于人工智能的超级计算机进行直接公共投资、加快数据中心规划审批，以及与全球超大规模云服务商建立牢固伙伴关系。荷兰则通过一体化追求战略相关性，将国家能力嵌入欧盟层面的算力、云和研究基础设施之中。

区别不在于雄心，而在于治理。英国政策强调国内控制和快速扩张算力；荷兰政策强调互操作性、协调以及共享的欧洲资产。

在英国，政策释放了大规模公共和私人投资。政府已承诺投入数十亿英镑资金，到2030年将人工智能算力扩大二十倍，设立了中央协调机构（包括一个主权人工智能部门），并吸引了超大规模云服务商和数据中心的大型投资。这巩固了英国作为欧洲领先的人工智能优化算力基础设施枢纽的地位，同时促进了硬件设计、冷却和模块化数据中心系统方面的创新。然而，快速扩张也暴露出碎片化、公共算力超额认购、电网瓶颈和技能短缺等问题。

荷兰侧重于协调供给而非规模。通过 AINed、SURF 和荷兰人工智能联盟（AIC4NL）提供的公共资金，支持算力共享访问、高性能计算（HPC）与云的有力整合，以及参与 EuroHPC。荷兰的优势在于世界一流的数字连接、节能基础设施和系统集成。结构性制约——电网容量有限、土地使用限制、资金缺口以及成长阶段融资较弱——限制了近期扩张，并增加了对欧盟层面资产的依赖。两国都面临人工智能、算力和能源系统技能方面的严重短缺。

两国都在投资以支持人工智能模型的训练和部署，但所走路径不同。英国正在建设前沿规模的国家系统，并配套商业云能力，将自身定位为训练和运行大型模型的地点。荷兰则更依赖欧盟规模的超算和联邦式访问，接受前沿算力将共享而非国家所有。

尽管存在这些差异，两国仍严重依赖美国超大规模云服务商，后者控制着可用人工智能算力的多数。共同制约十分严峻：电网拥堵、并网周期漫长、能源成本上升、规划限制和环境压力。数据中心选址日益受制于能源可获得性，而非需求。这些因素可能导致人工智能部署放缓、成本上升，并加深对外国基础设施的依赖。

英国和荷兰面临共同的战略挑战，包括规模化算力不足、能源和电网制约、技能短缺以及对非欧洲供应商的依赖。这些共同压力为双边合作创造了明确机遇。优先领域包括：统一可持续数据中心标准；协调高端算力获取；在人才发展上采取联合方式；以及探索跨境、与能源相联的算力解决方案，尤其是在北海。合作将增强韧性、减少重复建设，并巩固欧洲在人工智能领域的战略地位。

英国和荷兰的算力政策在意图上一致，但在执行上存在分歧。在英国，《国家人工智能战略》《现代工业战略》和《数字与技术行业计划》都将数据和算力资源列为人工智能领导地位的基础，以及全国生产力的关键使能因素。英国《算力路线图》承诺到2030年投入20亿英镑，建设一个“现代公共算力生态系统”，主要面向人工智能。总体而言，英国将算力视为主权能力和增长杠杆，投入大量公共资本，进行中央协调并推动规划改革，以加速算力建设。荷兰则将算力嵌入欧盟框架，优先考虑互操作性、共享基础设施和战略相关性，而非国家所有。欧盟立法，如《云与人工智能发展法案》（CADA），正通过全欧洲的努力，推动人工智能在荷兰的普及和云的采用。与此同时，荷兰的国家努力，如《人工智能战略行动计划》，强调算力和数据资源与技能、研究一样，对发展荷兰人工智能经济至关重要。

两种路径都面临制约。在英国，公共、学术和商业算力之间彼此割裂，国家资源超额认购，电网延迟和技能短缺，可能限制投资回报。在荷兰，资金受限、土地使用限制、电网饱和以及获取前沿规模算力的渠道有限，制约了可扩展性。两个生态系统都仍然面临依赖美国超大规模云服务商的风险。

这些差异之所以重要，是因为它们具有互补性。英国的规模和资本调动能力，与荷兰在协调、互联互通和欧盟一体化方面的优势相结合，能够形成良好互补。在标准、访问模式、可持续性和人才方面进行更有意识的协调，可能比任一单独路径带来更强的集体韧性。

私人投资正在推动两国的算力扩张，但规模不同。英国已吸引异常庞大的超大规模云服务商和数据中心承诺，巩固其作为欧洲人工智能算力枢纽的角色，并支撑不断壮大的专业供应商生态系统。荷兰继续吸引主要参与者的投资，这得益于其连通性和可持续性资质，但扩张受到分区规划和电网限制的制约。行业面临共同障碍，包括高昂且波动的能源成本、电网接入延迟、土地稀缺、技能短缺以及对专有云生态系统的锁定。这些因素推高成本、减缓部署，并限制有竞争力的欧洲替代方案出现。

items.title: Mapping AI Ecosystems in the Netherlands and the United Kingdom
items.author: Manuel Hernandez Gonzalez
items.summary: This report maps UK and Dutch AI ecosystems, identifying collaboration opportunities in health, agrifood and compute. The UK offers scale, frontier research and investment; the Netherlands offers specialisation and public-private coordination.
items.body:
Opportunities for bilateral collaboration and action

ResearchPublished Oct 8, 2026

This research was sponsored by UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)

This report compares the UK and Netherlands AI ecosystems and identifies practical opportunities for bilateral collaboration. The countries are complementary rather than direct competitors: the UK offers scale, frontier research, investment and global reach, while the Netherlands offers industrial specialisation and public-private coordination. Priority areas are life sciences and health, agrifood and agritech, and compute infrastructure.

This report maps the artificial intelligence (AI) research and innovation ecosystems of the United Kingdom and the Netherlands and identifies opportunities for deeper bilateral collaboration. Drawing on desk research, policy analysis, scientometric and patent data and stakeholder engagement, it compares the countries’ ecosystem structures, capabilities, policy approaches and sectoral strengths.

The report examines three priority areas for collaboration: AI in the life sciences and health technologies, AI applications in agrifood and agritech, and compute and ICT infrastructure for AI. In life sciences, collaboration could link UK commercial and translational scale with Dutch clinical integration and validation strengths. In agrifood, it could combine UK research, sensing, robotics and biotechnology capabilities with Dutch leadership in applied innovation and deployment. In compute, it could connect UK strengths in software, model development and AI compute expansion with Dutch capabilities in hardware, connectivity and sustainable digital infrastructure.

The report identifies practical opportunities for bilateral capability building, joint innovation and scale-up, and longer-term cooperation on resilient and trusted AI infrastructure.

The UK has greater scale, global reach, frontier AI research capacity, private investment and commercial activity. The Netherlands has a smaller but highly connected ecosystem, underpinned by industrial specialisation, strong public–private coordination and integration with European research, innovation and regulatory frameworks. These differences create complementarity rather than direct competition.

Both prioritise AI-enabled productivity and growth, responsible innovation, resilient compute and data infrastructure, workforce capability, and international cooperation with trusted partners. This alignment provides a clear foundation for joint initiatives, particularly where collaboration can link UK scale and frontier capability with Dutch industrial testbeds, coordination mechanisms and EU connections.

In each country, translating research excellence and early-stage innovation into sustained domestic growth and widespread use remains challenging. Key obstacles include insufficient growth-stage finance; shortages of specialist, applied and interdisciplinary skills; and uneven AI uptake among SMEs and sector-specific users. Data availability and interoperability, access to large-scale and sovereign compute, reliance on non-European hyperscalers, and energy and grid capacity constraints further limit expansion. Addressing these shared barriers could be a practical focus for bilateral action on scale-up pathways, skills development, trusted infrastructure, data collaboration and responsible AI governance.

- Compute for AI: Developing bilateral dialogues on trusted and sustainable compute, covering interoperability, researcher mobility, federated learning, energy-efficient infrastructure and resilient access to AI compute.

- Life sciences and health: Establish joint UK-Netherlands initiatives on AI-enabled health technologies, including capability mapping, targeted researcher and clinician secondments, joint training on trustworthy clinical AI and regulatory dialogue on safety and data standards.

- Agrifood and agritech: Develop joint agrifood AI living labs and Horizon Europe bids linking UK research, sensing, robotics and biotechnology capabilities with Dutch deployment-ready agrifood systems. Shared pilots should test AI tools across greenhouse, horticultural and open-field farming contexts.

items.titleZh: 绘制荷兰与英国的人工智能生态系统图谱
zhParas: 双边合作与行动机遇
研究发布于2026年10月8日
本研究由英国外交、联邦和发展事务部（FCDO）资助
本报告比较了英国与荷兰的人工智能生态系统，并识别出双边合作的实际机遇。两国互补而非直接竞争：英国提供规模、前沿研究、投资和全球影响力，荷兰则提供产业专业化和公私协调。优先领域为生命科学与健康、农业食品与农业科技，以及计算基础设施。
本报告梳理了英国与荷兰的人工智能（AI）研究与创新生态系统，并识别出深化双边合作的机会。报告基于案头研究、政策分析、科学计量与专利数据以及利益相关方参与，比较了两国的生态系统结构、能力、政策方法和行业优势。

本报告考察了三个优先合作领域：生命科学与健康技术中的人工智能、农业食品与农业科技中的人工智能应用，以及面向人工智能的计算与信息通信技术基础设施。在生命科学领域，合作可将英国商业化和转化规模与荷兰临床整合和验证优势连接起来。在农业食品领域，合作可将英国的研究、传感、机器人技术和生物技术能力与荷兰在应用创新和部署方面的领先地位结合起来。在计算领域，合作可将英国在软件、模型开发和AI算力扩展方面的优势与荷兰在硬件、连接性和可持续数字基础设施方面的能力对接起来。
报告指出了在双边能力建设、联合创新与规模化，以及在具有韧性和可信的人工智能基础设施方面开展长期合作的实际机遇。
英国拥有更大的规模、全球影响力、前沿人工智能研究能力、私人投资和商业活动。荷兰的生态系统规模较小但高度互联，其基础是产业专业化、强有力的公私协调以及与欧洲研究、创新和监管框架的融合。这些差异带来的是互补性，而非直接竞争。
两国都将人工智能赋能的生产力与增长、负责任创新、有韧性的算力和数据基础设施、劳动力能力以及与可信伙伴的国际合作列为优先事项。这种一致性为联合倡议奠定了明确基础，尤其是在合作能够将英国的规模与前沿能力同荷兰的产业试验场、协调机制和欧盟联系对接起来时。

在两国，将卓越研究和早期创新转化为持续的国内增长和广泛应用仍然具有挑战性。主要障碍包括成长阶段融资不足；专业、应用和跨学科技能短缺；以及中小企业和特定行业用户对人工智能的采用不均衡。数据可用性与互操作性、获取大规模和主权算力、对非欧洲超大规模云服务商的依赖，以及能源和电网容量限制，进一步制约了扩张。应对这些共同障碍，可以成为双边在规模化路径、技能发展、可信基础设施、数据合作和负责任人工智能治理方面采取行动的实际重点。
- 人工智能算力：开展关于可信且可持续算力的双边对话，涵盖互操作性、研究人员流动、联邦学习、能效基础设施以及有韧性的人工智能算力获取。
- 生命科学与健康：建立英荷人工智能赋能健康技术的联合倡议，包括能力图谱、有针对性的研究人员和临床医生借调、可信临床人工智能联合培训，以及关于安全与数据标准的监管对话。
- 农业食品与农业科技：发展联合农业食品人工智能生活实验室，以及连接英国研究、传感、机器人和生物技术能力与荷兰可部署农业食品系统的“地平线欧洲”项目申请。共享试点应在温室、园艺和露地种植场景中测试人工智能工具。

items.title: B-21 Testing, Manufacturing Ramp Up: ‘We’re Moving Fast’
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: Northrop Grumman has broken ground on a major new production facility for the B-21 Raider, the company and the Air Force announced Oct. 6. The construction comes as a top service official said testing on the bomber is going well in the lead up to its planned introduction into the operational fleet in 2027. The post B-21 Testing, Manufacturing Ramp Up: ‘We’re Moving Fast’ appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Northrop Grumman has broken ground on a major new production facility for the B-21 Raider, the company and the Air Force announced Oct. 6. The construction comes as a top service official said testing on the bomber is going well in the lead up to its planned introduction into the operational fleet in 2027.

“It’s more than construction,” Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink wrote in a social media post. “We’re moving fast to build B-21s!”

The Air Force Test Center has likewise been moving quickly to test the bomber ahead of its introduction into service next year. Brig. Gen. Mark Massaro, head of the Air Force Test Center at Edwards Air Force Base, Calif., gave an enthusiastic thumbs-up when asked about the program at an Oct. 6 event. The aircraft first flew in 2023, and two bombers are currently known to be undergoing testing at the base.

“I can’t give you many details about specifics on how it’s going, but I am very closely tied into that program and have been getting regular updates,” Massaro said during a discussion hosted by AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies. “We are actively testing right now.”

Less than 30 miles away, Northrop is already building B-21s at its Air Force Plant 42 facility in Palmdale, Calif., but the new construction will add 1 million square feet of production space. Meink said it will be the “final assembly line” for new bombers.

In February, Air Force officials said they had agreed on a plan with Northrop to increase B-21 production capacity by 25 percent, using $4.5 billion from the “One Big Beautiful Bill” legislation passed in 2025. Northrop is also investing $2.5 billion of its own money in bolstering B-21 production, CEO Kathy Warden said in April.

The new groundbreaking, which occurred Sept. 29, is “a significant step toward expanding production capacity for the B-21 Raider and delivering combat capability to the Joint Force faster,” the service wrote in a photo caption provided of the groundbreaking.

“The B-21 team has established the foundation to accelerate production responsibly,” Col. Nicholas Jordan, B-21 Systems program director, Rapid Capabilities Office, said in an Oct. 8 statement. “This investment in Palmdale will provide the infrastructure, workforce, and manufacturing capacity needed to deliver the Raider to the Air Force at an increased rate.”

Increased production capacity is likely—but not confirmed—to lead to more B-21s overall. While the official program of record is for a minimum of 100 bombers, U.S. Strategic Command boss Adm. Richard Correll and U.S. Pacific Command head Adm. Samuel Paparo have advocated for a larger B-21 buy, and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth told lawmakers in April that the Air Force will need “a lot more” than 100 B-21s in the future.

The Air Force has yet to formally commit to more than 100 bombers, but top leaders have indicated they are open to doing so.

“At some point in the future, we’ll consider additional buys,” Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach told Air & Space Forces Magazine in July when asked about increasing the size of the future B-21 fleet. “One of the things we’re talking to Northrop about is how could we do that in a way that doesn’t stretch out.”

The U.S. military has said it wants its bombers to be delivered more quickly.

“The B-21 Raider is foundational to the Air Force’s future long-range strike capability, and this investment strengthens the industrial capacity required to field that capability faster,” Gen. Dale White, the Pentagon’s Critical Major Weapon Systems, said in an Oct. 8 statement.

Exactly how many the service may buy will likely come out with the Air Force’s 2028 budget request, expected in spring 2027, Air Force Deputy Chief of Staff for Plans and Programs Lt. Gen. David H. Tabor said earlier this year.

Meanwhile, at Edwards, the Air Force is pushing a novel approach to testing by having developmental test pilots fly alongside operational test pilots, the head of the Test Center said.

“One of the areas that we’re really getting into, which we have done in the past, but in a big way, we’re moving forward in programs like the B-21 … is that integrated test,” Massaro said, which is “making sure that the warfighter and our operators have earlier insight into a lot of the developmental test work to be able to get information to make comments and understanding of what things might need to change earlier in a development cycle, but then also influence and discuss how this is going to be operated best. You’re bringing that operator in earlier into the Test Center test execution phase.”

“That integrated test construct is something that we’ve been very much focused on more often in a lot more programs, and that is something on the B-21 that I would like to highlight,” he added.

items.titleZh: B-21测试、制造加速：“我们正在快速推进
zhParas: 诺斯罗普·格鲁曼公司已为B-21“突袭者”轰炸机的一座大型新生产设施破土动工，该公司和美国空军于10月6日宣布。此时，一位空军高级官员表示，在该轰炸机计划于2027年进入作战机队之前，其测试进展顺利。
这不仅仅是建设，”空军部长特洛伊·梅因克在社交媒体帖子中写道。“我们正在快速推进B-21的建造！
空军测试中心同样一直在加紧推进该轰炸机在明年服役前的测试。位于加利福尼亚州爱德华兹空军基地的空军测试中心负责人马克·马萨罗准将在10月6日的一次活动中被问及该项目时，热情地竖起了大拇指。该机于2023年首飞，目前已知有两架轰炸机正在该基地接受测试。
关于进展的具体细节，我不能透露太多，但我与该项目的联系非常紧密，并一直定期收到最新情况，”马萨罗在美国空军协会米切尔航空航天研究所主办的一场讨论中表示。“我们目前正在积极进行测试。
在不到30英里外，诺斯罗普公司已经在加利福尼亚州帕姆代尔的空军42号工厂建造B-21，但新建设施将增加100万平方英尺的生产空间。梅因克表示，这将成为新轰炸机的“总装线”。
今年2月，空军官员表示，他们已与诺斯罗普公司达成一项计划，利用2025年通过的“大而美法案”提供的45亿美元，将B-21产能提高25%。诺斯罗普公司首席执行官凯西·沃登在4月表示，该公司还自投25亿美元，用于加强B-21生产。
这次于9月29日举行的破土动工，是“扩大B-21‘突袭者’生产能力、更快向联合部队交付作战能力的重要一步”，空军在提供的一张破土动工照片说明中写道。
B-21团队已为负责任地加快生产奠定了基础，”快速能力办公室B-21系统项目主管尼古拉斯·乔丹上校在10月8日的一份声明中表示。“对帕姆代尔的这项投资将提供所需的基础设施、劳动力和制造能力，以更快的速度向空军交付‘突袭者’。
美国空军尚未正式承诺采购超过100架轰炸机，但高层领导人已表示愿意这样做。
未来某个时候，我们会考虑追加采购，”美国空军参谋长肯·威尔士巴赫上将在7月被问及是否扩大未来B-21机队规模时对《空军与太空军杂志》表示。“我们与诺斯罗普讨论的事项之一，就是如何以不拖长的方式做到这一点。
美军表示，希望其轰炸机能够更快交付。
B-21‘突袭者’是空军未来远程打击能力的基础，这项投资增强了更快部署该能力所需的工业产能，”五角大楼关键重大武器系统的戴尔·怀特将军在10月8日的一份声明中表示。
空军负责计划与项目的副参谋长戴维·H·塔博尔中将今年早些时候表示，空军究竟可能采购多少架，很可能将随空军2028财年预算申请一并公布，而该预算申请预计于2027年春季发布。
与此同时，在爱德华兹空军基地，空军正在推行一种新颖的测试方法，让研发试飞员与作战试飞员共同飞行，测试中心负责人表示。
我们真正深入涉足的一个领域——我们过去也做过，但现在是大力推进——在B-21等项目上正在向前推进……就是一体化测试，”马萨罗说，这“确保作战人员和我们的使用人员能更早深入了解大量研发测试工作，从而获取信息，在研发周期更早阶段就哪些方面可能需要改变提出意见并形成理解，同时还能影响并讨论如何以最佳方式运用该系统。也就是让使用人员在更早阶段就进入测试中心的测试执行阶段。
这种一体化测试架构是我们近年来在更多项目中更频繁、也非常重点关注的事项，而这也是我想在B-21项目上特别强调的一点，”他补充道。
编者按：本文于10月8日更新，补充了更多信息。

items.title: Air Force Mulls Adding a Missile Warning System to F-15EX
items.author: Steve Losey
items.summary: The Air Force is looking for ways to add an integrated missile warning system into the F-15EX Eagle II fighter for the first time. The post Air Force Mulls Adding a Missile Warning System to F-15EX appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
The Air Force is looking for ways to add an integrated missile warning system into the F-15EX Eagle II fighter for the first time.

The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center posted a sources sought notice Sept. 29 as part of a market research effort, looking for potential vendors for a missile launch and approach warning system that could be quickly installed on the F-15EX.

The system has to be able to alert the fighter’s aircrew about missile threats without distracting them with too many false alarms, the notice states. It also has to use the F-15EX’s six preexisting sensor locations already earmarked for missile warning, as well as the jet’s data cables, power cables and cooling capabilities. And it has to be able to be quickly and easily installed or removed in the field by Air Force maintainers, without requiring any changes to the aircraft itself aside from installing line replaceable units in the six sensor locations, per the notive.

The notice did not say how much such a system could cost or how long the contract could last, but said those details will be in line with what such work typically requires.

The Boeing-made F-15EX is a more advanced version of the F-15E Strike Eagle, with upgrades including fly-by-wire controls and a new electronic warfare system. But while the jets are built with the features necessary for a missile warning system, they do not actually come with that capability, even though other variants like Saudi Arabia’s F-15SA and Qatar’s F-15QA do.

The F-15EX does have the Eagle Passive Active Warning Survivability System, an advanced electronic warfare suite that can jam enemies’ radar systems and thus defend against radar-guided missiles. But a new missile warning system would help defend against infrared-guided vehicles.

Other Air Force fighters have missile warning systems that can detect infrared-guided threats—the F-35 has the AN/AAQ-37 Distributed Aperture System, built by Northrop Grumman, and the F-22 has the AN/AAR-56 Missile Launch Detection system.

Years ago, the F-15C was supposed to be equipped under the Common Missile Warning System, a joint program between the Army, Navy, and Air Force. But the Air Force dropped out of that program in 2000, according to a report from the Institute for Defense Analyses. The Common Missile Warning System eventually became the AN/AAR-57, built by BAE Systems. The F-15SA has the CMWS from BAE.

The threat of infrared-guided missiles was underscored during Operation Epic Fury, when an F-15E Strike Eagle, the EX’s predecessor, was downed over Iran in April. President Donald Trump said Iran used a shoulder-fired missile—often called a man-portable air defense system or MANPADS—to hit the fighter, and MANPADS often use infrared sensors.

While the Air Force is not committing to buying a new system, the request shows it is giving serious consideration to adding it at a time when the service’s plans for the F-15EX are rapidly expanding. Just this past April, the Air Force announced it was expanding its planned fleet size from 129 aircraft to 269.

AFLCMC wants potential respondents to say what military aircraft their missile warning systems are already approved on for operational use, whether the system is currently in active production, and how many months after the contract award could the companies start delivering the system, among other issues.

Companies have until Nov. 12 to submit unclassified white papers on their systems’ technical capabilities to the Air Force.
items.titleZh: 空军正在研究为F-15EX“鹰II”战斗机配备集成式导弹预警系统的可能性。
items.summaryZh: 空军正在探索首次在F-15EX“鹰II”战斗机上配备集成式导弹预警系统的方法。该报道最初发表于《航空与太空部队杂志》。
zhParas: 空军正在探索首次在F-15EX“鹰II”战斗机上配备集成式导弹预警系统的方法。
9月29日，空军生命周期管理中心发布了寻源公告，开展市场调研工作，旨在为F-15EX战斗机寻找能够快速安装的导弹发射与逼近预警系统供应商。
根据相关公告，该导弹预警系统必须能够在向战机乘员发出导弹威胁警报的同时，避免因过多误报而干扰他们的操作。此外，该系统还需利用F-15EX上已为导弹预警预留的六个传感器位置，以及飞机的数据电缆、电源电缆和冷却系统。同时，公告要求该系统必须能由空军维护人员快速、便捷地在现场安装或拆除，且除在六个传感器位置更换可更换式组件外，无需对飞机本身进行任何其他改动。
该公告并未透露此类导弹预警系统的造价或合同期限，仅表示相关细节将按照此类项目的常规要求来确定。
由波音公司制造的F-15EX是F-15E“打击之鹰”战机的升级版，配备了电传操纵系统以及全新的电子战系统等改进措施。尽管这款战机在结构设计上具备安装导弹预警系统所需的条件，但实际上并未配备该功能，而沙特阿拉伯的F-15SA和卡塔尔的F-15QA等其他型号则已具备这一能力。
虽然F-15EX已配备“鹰式被动主动预警生存系统”这一先进的电子战装置，该系统可通过干扰敌方雷达系统来抵御雷达制导的导弹，但新的导弹预警系统将有助于防范红外制导的武器威胁。
其他型号的空军战机也配备了能够探测红外制导威胁的导弹预警系统——诺斯罗普·格鲁曼公司制造的F-35配备了AN/AAQ-37分布式孔径系统，而F-22则搭载有AN/AAR-56导弹发射检测系统。
据国防分析研究所的报道，多年前F-15C原本应配备由陆军、海军和空军共同推行的“通用导弹预警系统”。但根据相关记录，空军在2000年便退出了该计划。该“通用导弹预警系统”最终发展为由BAE系统公司研发的AN/AAR-57导弹预警系统，而F-15SA型号则配备了BAE公司生产的CMWS导弹预警系统。
在“史诗怒火”行动期间，红外制导导弹的威胁愈发凸显——该行动发生于4月，F-15E“打击鹰”战斗机（即F-15EX的前身）在伊朗上空被击落。唐纳德·特朗普总统称，伊朗使用了肩扛式导弹击落了这架战斗机，而这类导弹通常被称为便携式防空系统，其往往依赖红外传感器来锁定目标。
尽管空军尚未正式决定采购新的导弹预警系统，但这一需求表明，随着F-15EX战机的部署计划不断加速推进，军方正在认真考虑为其配备该系统。就在今年4月，空军就宣布计划将F-15EX战机的数量从129架增至269架。
美军印太司令部希望潜在的投标企业详细说明其导弹预警系统目前已获批准用于哪些军用飞机、该系统是否处于量产阶段，以及在合同签订后多少个月内能够开始交付系统，同时还要求企业提供其他相关信息。
各企业必须在11月12日前向空军提交关于其系统技术性能的未涉密白皮书。

尽管空军尚未正式决定采购新的导弹预警系统，但这一需求表明，随着F-15EX战机的部署计划不断加速推进，军方正在认真考虑为其配备该系统。就在今年4月，空军就宣布计划将F-15EX战机的数量从129架增至269架。

美军印太司令部希望潜在的投标企业详细说明其导弹预警系统目前已获批准用于哪些军用飞机、该系统是否处于量产阶段，以及在合同签订后多少个月内能够开始交付系统，同时还要求企业提供其他相关信息。

各企业必须在11月12日前向空军提交关于其系统技术性能的未涉密白皮书。

items.title: With OCX Axed, Space Force Moves Forward with New GPS Ground Plan
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: After scrapping a long-delayed program to build a next-generation GPS ground system earlier this year, the Space Force and prime contractor Lockheed Martin are pushing toward delivery of the capability in time to support the first launch of the newest GPS satellites, currently planned for 2028. The post With OCX Axed, Space Force Moves Forward with New GPS Ground Plan appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
After scrapping a long-delayed program to build a next-generation GPS ground system earlier this year, the Space Force and prime contractor Lockheed Martin are pushing toward delivery of the capability in time to support the first launch of the newest GPS satellites, currently planned for 2028.

However, a new report from the Government Accountability Office raises concerns about that timeline. Further, the Space Force still lacks a plan to operationalize a key civilian signal installed in GPS satellites already on orbit. That signal, called L5, provides higher bandwidth and is more resistant to jamming and interference than other civilian GPS signals—which is important for aviation and maritime safety.

The Space Force announced in April it would cancel its long troubled Next-Generation GPS Operational Control Segment, or OCX. The system was meant to operate “Generation 3” satellites, to include the GPS III and GPS IIIF variants. But the effort, led by prime contractor RTX, failed to meet cost and schedule targets. By the time the Space Force pulled the plug, the program was 10 years late and its cost had nearly doubled from $3.7 billion to $6.27 billion.

Erin Carper, the acting portfolio acquisition executive for positioning, navigation, and timing and satellite communications, told reporters in September the decision to cancel OCX after more than 15 years and billions of dollars was driven primarily by two imperatives: the need to deliver the ground control elements for GPS IIIF satellites on time and to contain development risk along the way.

“Can we do it faster and not perturb the IIIF schedule? That was a significant driver,” Carper said Sept. 15 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference. “And then the other thing was, do we understand the risk remaining? The test campaign for OCX and the burn down of [deficiency reports] and some of the other things, that’s where we saw risk to the schedule for OCX.”

Rather than continue with OCX, the service opted instead to funnel resources toward a series of upgrades Lockheed Martin has been delivering for the legacy GPS ground segment, dubbed the Architecture Evolution Program, or AEP. The service first put Lockheed on contract for AEP in 2016, when OCX was delayed, to ensure the ground system could support GPS III launches and, eventually, command and control them once on orbit.

Since April, the Space Force has awarded Lockheed an additional $199 million to upgrade AEP to support launch and command and control for GPS IIIF satellites—an effort it’s calling AEP-M—and to begin a full technology refresh of the GPS ground segment hardware and software. That upgrade will lay the foundation for the next generation of the GPS ground system, known as Gen4. The service envisions that architecture as more modular and distributed, and it’s considering how it might leverage commercial antennas and other capabilities to support it.

Lockheed’s Vice President for Global Communications and Navigation Christina Mancinelli said that over the last 10 years, the company has completed more than 100 projects aimed at adding new capabilities to AEP, including a capability called M-Code Early Use, which allowed the ground system to task and monitor an advanced, secure signal called M-Code.

“We’ve been modernizing along the way,” Mancinelli said. “There have been some big upgrades we’ve made on the ground, but we have also been evolving it and doing projects to keep up with things for the last decade.”

Both Mancinelli and Carper said their teams are pushing to have AEP-M ready for the first GPS IIIF launch, though they noted that they’re still negotiating a formal schedule for the effort. A Space Systems Command spokesperson said the schedule is currently under review by the Pentagon’s Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation office. They declined to give an estimate of when the timeline might be solidified and wouldn’t provide a total cost estimate for the effort.

Meanwhile, GAO said in an Oct. 7 report that to support a 2028 launch, the ground control capability must be available by early 2027.

More broadly, Carper said she’s optimistic that Lockheed’s heritage on GPS ground and the program’s more incremental approach will help it avoid some of the pitfalls of OCX, which was attempting to pull off what she described as “a big bang delivery of capability.” In modern software development, incremental deliveries are favored because if there’s a glitch in an update, it’s easier to revert, or roll back, to a more stable version of the software to address it.

“There’s significant risk in cutting an entire constellation of operational satellites over to a brand new ground system, and that meant a level of test and oversight that was becoming very challenging,” she said. “With AEP-M, we’re able to roll out incremental capabilities, roll back more easily. … That’s not to say there aren’t inherent risks; there always will be. We will run into challenges, but we understand what some of those challenges are and are managing the risk.”

While the AEP-M contracts awarded to date cover the scope of what OCX would have provided for command and control and launch support, it doesn’t include modifications needed to operationalize the L5 signal. That signal is installed today on 21 spacecraft—some older GPS IIFs as well as all 10 GPS III satellites in orbit. However, due to OCX delays, the service hasn’t yet upgraded the ground system to monitor those signals.

SSC confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine that it has not yet awarded a contract for the L5 signal upgrades.

“The L5 effort was not included in the recently awarded control segment contracts to Lockheed,” a Space Systems Command spokesperson said. “The Space Force is focused on delivering capability incrementally as quickly as possible and is exploring all appropriate options for delivering modernized civil signals.”

SSC noted that it’s working with the Department of Transportation and the Federal Aviation Administration to finalize a plan for that work and expects to award contracts “in the near future.”

Amid a rise in GPS jamming and spoofing incidents in recent years, experts and commercial industry have been pushing for the U.S. government to operationalize the L5 signal—a move they say would make the aviation industry and commercial receivers more resilient. In 2024, the GPS Innovation Alliance recommended the Defense Department “increase the urgency and primacy” of upgrading the GPS ground system to support more robust civil signals.

“The more you can integrate multiple different types of signals into a receiver as well as combine that with specialized antennas … the better you are at resisting attempts to jam or spoof your receiver or device,” Lisa Dyer, the alliance’s executive director, told Air & Space Forces Magazine on Oct. 7. “We see today a need for that kind of capability, and L5 is one of those signals that we’d really like to see get integrated as soon as possible.”

There are other complicating factors beyond the ground system upgrade plans, including a requirement that at least 24 satellites be broadcasting the signal before it can be declared fully operational. Some commercial firms have already integrated L5 into their operations, but more regulated industries like aviation need the FAA to certify the signal as healthy before they can follow suit.

It’s possible the FAA could approve the signal before it hits the 24-satellite threshold, but one source familiar with the discussions said the agency is unlikely to change its position or permit waivers due to safety concerns. There has also been discussion around fielding the first GPS IIIF satellites on a faster timeline, but it’s unclear if there would be room on the launch manifest to accelerate the program due to current bottlenecks in the launch industry. And according to the GAO report, even if the Space Force and Lockheed were able to accelerate IIIF deliveries, there’s no certainty that the ground segment would be ready to support an earlier launch.
items.titleZh: 在原有GPS地面系统计划被取消后，美国太空军加快推进新型GPS地面系统建设
items.summaryZh: 在今年早些时候放弃那个长期拖延、旨在打造新一代GPS地面系统的计划之后，美国太空军与主要承包商洛克希德·马丁公司正在加紧推进相关工作的完成，力求在2028年计划发射的首批新型GPS卫星升空之际，让这一系统能够及时投入使用。
zhParas: 在今年早些时候放弃那个长期拖延、旨在打造新一代GPS地面系统的计划之后，美国太空军与主要承包商洛克希德·马丁公司正在加紧推进相关工作的完成，力求在2028年计划发射的首批新型GPS卫星升空之际，让这一系统能够及时投入使用。
不过，美国政府问责局发布的一份新报告对这一时间表提出了质疑。此外，美国太空军目前仍缺乏针对已部署在轨道上的GPS卫星中所使用的某项关键民用信号的启用计划。该信号被称为L5，相比其他民用GPS信号，它具有更高的带宽，且更不易受到干扰，这对于保障航空与海上安全至关重要。
太空军于4月宣布取消长期面临困境的下一代GPS运行控制模块项目。该系统原本用于为包括GPS III和GPS IIIF型号在内的“第三代”GPS卫星提供支持，但由主要承包商RTX主导的这项工作始终无法实现成本与时间目标。到太空军最终终止该计划时，项目已延误10年，其成本也从37亿美元上升了近一倍，达到62.7亿美元。
负责定位、导航、计时及卫星通信事务的临时项目采购主管埃琳·卡珀在9月向记者表示，经过15年多的时间以及数十亿美元的投入后最终决定取消OCX项目，主要是出于两方面的考量：一是必须按时为GPS IIIF卫星提供地面控制设备，二是要控制项目开发过程中的各种风险。
卡珀在9月15日举行的AFA航空、航天与网络会议上表示：‘我们能否加快速度推进工作，同时又不影响GPS IIIF卫星项目的进度？这其实是推动我们做出决策的重要因素。’她还指出，‘另一个需要考虑的点是，我们是否清楚仍存在的风险？OCX项目的测试工作、各类缺陷报告的处理以及其它相关事务，都可能对项目的进度造成威胁。’
由于决定放弃OCX项目，该军种选择将资源投入到洛克希德·马丁公司正在为旧版GPS地面系统推进的一系列升级工作中，该计划被称为“架构演进计划”或AEP。早在2016年OCX项目出现延误时，为确保地面系统能够为GPS III卫星的发射提供支持，并在卫星入轨后实现对其的指挥控制，该军种便首次与洛克希德·马丁公司签订了AEP项目的合同。

自4月以来，美国太空军已再向洛克希德·马丁公司拨款1.99亿美元，用于升级“架构演进计划”，以便为GPS IIIF卫星的发射及指挥控制提供支持——该升级项目被命名为“AEP-M”；同时这笔资金还将用于对GPS地面系统的硬件与软件进行全面技术更新。此次升级将为下一代GPS地面系统（即第四代系统）奠定基础。太空军期望这一新架构具备更高的模块化与分布式特性，并正在研究如何利用商用天线及其他技术手段来支撑该系统的运行。
洛克希德·马丁公司全球通信与导航业务副总裁克里斯蒂娜·曼奇内利表示，过去10年间该公司已完成了100多个旨在为“AEP”系统增添新功能的项目，其中包括名为“M-Code早期应用”的功能，该功能能够让地面系统发送指令并监测一种名为M-Code的先进加密信号。
曼奇内利表示：‘我们一直在对系统进行现代化改造。过去十年间，我们不仅对地面设施进行了多项重大升级，还持续推动系统发展并开展各类项目，以确保其始终能跟上技术发展的步伐。’
曼奇内利与卡珀均表示，他们的团队正在加紧推进AEP-M系统的研发，以便能及时用于首批GPS IIIF卫星的发射，不过他们同时指出目前仍在商讨该项目的正式时间表。太空系统司令部的一位发言人称，该时间表目前正由五角大楼的成本评估与项目评估办公室进行审核。他们既不愿透露时间表何时能最终确定，也不愿提供该项目的总成本估算。
美国政府问责局在10月7日发布的报告中指出，为保障2028年的卫星发射任务，相关的地面控制系统必须在2027年初之前建成并投入使用。
卡珀表示，她对洛克希德在GPS地面系统建设方面的丰富经验以及该计划采用的渐进式推进方式充满信心，这些优势有望帮助其避免OCX计划所遭遇的种种问题——后者试图以她所称的“一次性全面交付”的方式来实现目标。在现代软件开发中，人们更倾向于采用渐进式交付方式，因为一旦某个更新中出现故障，就可以更容易地回退到更稳定的软件版本来解决问题。
她表示，将整个在役卫星群全部切换到全新的地面系统存在巨大风险，这也意味着需要进行大量的测试并实施严格的监管，工作难度极高。通过AEP-M方案，我们可以分阶段逐步推出新功能，出现问题时也能更轻松地回退到旧版本。当然这并非说没有固有风险——风险始终存在。我们确实会面临各种挑战，但已经清楚其中的一些问题，并正在采取措施控制风险。
目前所签订的AEP-M合同虽涵盖了OCX计划承担的指挥控制与发射支持功能，但并未包含让L5信号能够投入实际使用所需的改造工作。目前已有21颗航天器配备了这一L5信号，其中包括一些较老的GPS IIF系列卫星以及目前在轨运行的全部10颗GPS III系列卫星。但由于OCX项目的延误，地面系统至今仍未升级，无法对这些信号进行监测。
《航空与太空部队杂志》从太空军方面获悉，该军目前尚未就L5信号的升级项目下达任何合同。
太空系统司令部的一位发言人表示，近期授予洛克希德公司的控制段合同并未包含L5信号升级项目。太空军正致力于尽快分阶段实现相关能力，并正在探索各种合适方案，以提供现代化的民用信号服务。
SOCOM表示，其正在与美国交通部及联邦航空管理局合作，最终确定相关实施计划，并预计将在“不久的将来”授予相关合同。
近年来，随着GPS干扰和信号欺骗事件日益增多，专家们及商业行业一直在敦促美国政府启用L5信号，他们认为此举将提升航空业及各类商用接收设备的抗干扰能力。2024年，GPS创新联盟建议国防部加快升级GPS地面系统的工作进度，提升其优先级，从而为民用领域提供更可靠的信号支持。
该联盟的执行主任丽莎·戴尔在10月7日接受《航空与航天力量杂志》采访时指出：“如果能在接收器中整合更多不同类型的信号，并再搭配专用天线，那么抵御干扰或信号欺骗的能力就会越强。”她进一步表示：“目前我们确实需要这样的能力，而L5信号正是我们希望尽快得以整合进接收系统中的候选信号之一。
除了地面系统升级计划之外，还有其他一些复杂因素。根据相关规定，只有在至少24颗卫星开始发射该信号后，该系统才能被宣布全面投入运行。目前已有部分商业企业将L5信号纳入了自身的业务系统中，但航空业这类受更多监管的行业，则需要先获得美国联邦航空管理局对该信号稳定性的认证，才能随之采用这一技术。

有消息称美国联邦航空管理局或许会在卫星数量尚未达到24颗的节点前批准该信号，但一位了解相关讨论的人士表示，出于安全考虑，该机构不太可能改变立场或批准特例。此外也有意见提议加快首批GPS IIIF卫星的部署速度，但由于当前航天发射行业存在诸多瓶颈，尚不确定是否能有足够的发射名额来推进这一计划。根据美国政府问责局的报告，即便太空军与洛克希德·马丁公司能够加快IIIF卫星的交付速度，也无法保证地面系统能及时准备就绪，以支持更早的发射任务。

曼奇内利与卡珀均表示，他们的团队正在加紧推进AEP-M系统的研发，以便能及时用于首批GPS IIIF卫星的发射，不过他们同时指出目前仍在商讨该项目的正式时间表。太空系统司令部的一位发言人称，该时间表目前正由五角大楼的成本评估与项目评估办公室进行审核。他们既不愿透露时间表何时能最终确定，也不愿提供该项目的总成本估算。

美国政府问责局在10月7日发布的报告中指出，为保障2028年的卫星发射任务，相关的地面控制系统必须在2027年初之前建成并投入使用。

卡珀表示，她对洛克希德在GPS地面系统建设方面的丰富经验以及该计划采用的渐进式推进方式充满信心，这些优势有望帮助其避免OCX计划所遭遇的种种问题——后者试图以她所称的“一次性全面交付”的方式来实现目标。在现代软件开发中，人们更倾向于采用渐进式交付方式，因为一旦某个更新中出现故障，就可以更容易地回退到更稳定的软件版本来解决问题。

她表示，将整个在役卫星群全部切换到全新的地面系统存在巨大风险，这也意味着需要进行大量的测试并实施严格的监管，工作难度极高。通过AEP-M方案，我们可以分阶段逐步推出新功能，出现问题时也能更轻松地回退到旧版本。当然这并非说没有固有风险——风险始终存在。我们确实会面临各种挑战，但已经清楚其中的一些问题，并正在采取措施控制风险。

目前所签订的AEP-M合同虽涵盖了OCX计划承担的指挥控制与发射支持功能，但并未包含让L5信号能够投入实际使用所需的改造工作。目前已有21颗航天器配备了这一L5信号，其中包括一些较老的GPS IIF系列卫星以及目前在轨运行的全部10颗GPS III系列卫星。但由于OCX项目的延误，地面系统至今仍未升级，无法对这些信号进行监测。

《航空与太空部队杂志》从太空军方面获悉，该军目前尚未就L5信号的升级项目下达任何合同。

太空系统司令部的一位发言人表示，近期授予洛克希德公司的控制段合同并未包含L5信号升级项目。太空军正致力于尽快分阶段实现相关能力，并正在探索各种合适方案，以提供现代化的民用信号服务。

SOCOM表示，其正在与美国交通部及联邦航空管理局合作，最终确定相关实施计划，并预计将在“不久的将来”授予相关合同。

近年来，随着GPS干扰和信号欺骗事件日益增多，专家们及商业行业一直在敦促美国政府启用L5信号，他们认为此举将提升航空业及各类商用接收设备的抗干扰能力。2024年，GPS创新联盟建议国防部加快升级GPS地面系统的工作进度，提升其优先级，从而为民用领域提供更可靠的信号支持。

该联盟的执行主任丽莎·戴尔在10月7日接受《航空与航天力量杂志》采访时指出：“如果能在接收器中整合更多不同类型的信号，并再搭配专用天线，那么抵御干扰或信号欺骗的能力就会越强。”她进一步表示：“目前我们确实需要这样的能力，而L5信号正是我们希望尽快得以整合进接收系统中的候选信号之一。

除了地面系统升级计划之外，还有其他一些复杂因素。根据相关规定，只有在至少24颗卫星开始发射该信号后，该系统才能被宣布全面投入运行。目前已有部分商业企业将L5信号纳入了自身的业务系统中，但航空业这类受更多监管的行业，则需要先获得美国联邦航空管理局对该信号稳定性的认证，才能随之采用这一技术。

有消息称美国联邦航空管理局或许会在卫星数量尚未达到24颗的节点前批准该信号，但一位了解相关讨论的人士表示，出于安全考虑，该机构不太可能改变立场或批准特例。此外也有意见提议加快首批GPS IIIF卫星的部署速度，但由于当前航天发射行业存在诸多瓶颈，尚不确定是否能有足够的发射名额来推进这一计划。根据美国政府问责局的报告，即便太空军与洛克希德·马丁公司能够加快IIIF卫星的交付速度，也无法保证地面系统能及时准备就绪，以支持更早的发射任务。

items.title: Rubio says US, Greece to jointly combat security threats
items.author: Ivana Sekularac, Angeliki Koutantou, Lefteris Papadimas, Jonathan Landay, Reuters
items.summary: The U.S. and Greece are launching a joint security program to strengthen counterterrorism information sharing between their law enforcement agencies.
items.body:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that “strong and model NATO ally” Greece and the United States are launching new counterterrorism information sharing between their law enforcement agencies.

During an official visit to Athens, Rubio said Greece was particularly exposed to the threats posed by mass migration and human trafficking.

“As part of our efforts to combat these common threats to our nations, we’re proud to announce a new memorandum of understanding establishing a joint security program to strengthen the counterterrorism information sharing between our respective law enforcement agencies,” he told reporters alongside Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis.

Greece has been an important NATO ally to the United States, offering key military facilities to safeguard security in the Eastern Mediterranean, and it leads an EU maritime mission to protect commercial shipping in the Red Sea.

Rubio and Gerapetritis presided over the sixth round of a U.S.-Greece strategic dialogue that began in 2018 in which the sides agreed “to deepen defense ties, bolster trade and investment, and promote cultural ties,” according to a joint statement.

Greece, it said, would receive $4 billion to support a long-term defense plan to increase interoperability between the two militaries and to “explore future opportunities for defense industrial base cooperation.”

Gerapetritis said that Greece was willing to cooperate with the United States and offer maritime aid in the Strait of Hormuz if there is a viable peace process there.

Rubio stood by U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after U.S. senators expressed concerns over allegations that she had threatened that the U.S. could use its influence to undermine the Greek government.

Asked if her conduct was in compliance with State Department ethics, Rubio said: “Suffice it to say, our embassy here is doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”
items.titleZh: 卢比奥称美希将携手应对安全威胁
items.summaryZh: 美国与希腊正在推出一项联合安全计划，旨在加强两国执法机构之间的反恐信息共享机制。
zhParas: 美国国务卿马可·卢比奥周三表示，作为‘强大且堪称典范的北约盟友’的希腊与美国正在推动两国执法机构之间开展新的反恐信息共享机制。
在雅典的正式访问期间，卢比奥表示，希腊尤其面临大规模移民和人口贩卖所带来的安全威胁。
在与希腊外交部长乔治·格拉佩特里蒂斯一同接受记者采访时，卢比奥表示：‘为共同应对这些威胁两国安全的共同挑战，我们很高兴宣布达成一项新的谅解备忘录，旨在建立一项联合安全计划，从而加强两国执法机构在反恐信息共享方面的合作。’
作为美国重要的北约盟友，希腊不仅提供关键的军事设施以维护东地中海地区的安全，还牵头开展欧盟海上任务，旨在保护红海地区的商业航运安全。
根据双方发布的联合声明，鲁比奥与格拉佩特里蒂斯共同主持了始于2018年的第六轮美希战略对话。在会谈中，双方同意“深化防务合作，加强贸易与投资往来，并促进文化交流”。
据称，希腊将获得40亿美元资金，用于支持一项长期国防计划，旨在提升两国军队的协同作战能力，并“探索国防工业领域未来的合作机遇”。
格拉佩特里蒂斯表示，如果霍尔木兹海峡能够启动可行的和平进程，希腊愿与美国携手合作，并为该地区的安全保障提供海上援助。
在多名美国参议员对金伯利·吉尔福伊尔涉嫌威胁称美国会利用自身影响力削弱希腊政府表示担忧后，鲁比奥站出来为这位美国驻希腊大使辩护。
当被问及她的行为是否符合美国国务院的道德规范时，鲁比奥回应称：‘可以说，我们在这里的大使馆工作表现极为出色，我们的大使也是一位非常出色的驻希腊大使。’

items.title: Air Force Leaders Elevate Point Defense as a Key Air Warfare Mission
items.author: Matthew Cox
items.summary: Flying and fixing aircraft remains the Air Force’s reason for being, but protecting air bases from attack is becoming an essential component that makes those possible. Following attacks on air bases across the Middle East during Operation Epic Fury, point defense was among the hottest topics on tap at AFA’s 2026 Air, Space and Cyber conference in September. The post Air Force Leaders Elevate Point Defense as a Key Air Warfare Mission appeared first on <a href="https://www.air
items.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Flying and fixing aircraft remains the Air Force’s reason for being, but protecting air bases from attack is becoming an essential component that makes those possible. Following attacks on air bases across the Middle East during Operation Epic Fury, point defense was among the hottest topics on tap at AFA’s 2026 Air, Space and Cyber conference in September.

The Iranian attacks, such as the March 27 air raid on Prince Sultan Air Base, Saudi Arabia that damaged multiple refueling aircraft and an E-3 Sentry AWACS command and control plane, did not deliver crippling blows. But they did cause injuries, disrupt operations, and destroy some aircraft.

The damage was great enough to convince Air Force leaders to prioritize air base defense—or point defense, as they are calling it—and invest in new weapons and a new career field to man them.

Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink and Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach announced new initiatives at the conference, aimed at improving oversight of point defense acquisitions amid the recent explosion of growth in the counter-drone industry as it responds to increasing Pentagon demand.

Wilsbach pledged that point defense will no longer be treated as a “side hustle” but as a “core function of air and space power.”

The Air Force began ramping up its point defense strategy in late 2023 after unidentified drones were seen flying repeatedly over Langley Air Force Base, Va. Soon the service, along with the rest of the U.S. military, was racing to catch up with the rapidly evolving drone warfare threats and tactics emerging from the war in Ukraine. Then in June 2025, Operation Spider Web, a bold Ukrainian drone attack on strategic bomber bases deep inside Russia, showed Air Force leaders just how vulnerable the service’s own air bases were to this new threat.

But it took the hard lessons from a shooting war with Iran to elevate point defense to a new level of importance at the service’s semiannual Corona summit in June and make it a key focus at this year’s AFA event, said retired Air Force Lt. Gen. David Deptula, dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies.

“The reason why it was announced at AFA is because a decision had been made at the previous Corona to make point defense a mission function of the Air Force,” Deptula said. The conference “was the first opportunity to really make a big splash.”

During the conference, several Air Force generals said that the service’s increased emphasis on point defense is needed after watching Iranian drone and missile attacks strike air bases during Epic Fury.

Air Combat Command Boss Gen. Adrian L. Spain said Epic Fury “laid bare some of those things that have been in front of us for a while, and it just reminded us that we have to get after some of these things.”

“Our bases are under attack; we have to continue to generate air power in spite of that,” Spain said. “We have to be able to be resilient under attack, and we have to be able to sustain the force under those kinds of pressures to win.”

The Air Force’s chief modernization officer, Lt. Gen. Christopher J. Niemi, said the service identified more than a year ago that it would have to “increasingly protect our assets at air bases with investments in point defense but that accelerated … because of some of the experiences that we had over there.”

Prior to Epic Fury, the Air Force appeared to be banking on its agile combat employment strategy to disperse forces from large bases to ad hoc air bases in order to complicate targeting for adversaries and fight through attacks. The service evacuated Al Udeid Air Base, Qatar, before the Feb. 28 launch of Epic Fury, moving aircraft and most personnel to other locations both in the region and back in the United States.

When Iranian forces attacked Al Udeid, destroying the Combined Air Operations Center, or CAOC, there, the facility was empty—the first time it hadn’t participated in air combat operations since the 1990s. Instead, Epic Fury’s air operations were commanded fromShaw Air Force Base, S.C.

“ACE was really birthed out of necessity, [because] I cannot protect these forces any longer,” Spain said. “But if I could perfectly protect all my forces at a location, I would not move. There’s no reason to move. I’m only creating turbulence for myself if I do that.” That turbulence extends to every part of an air operation, he said: “I have a logistics problem I’ve got to worry about. I’ve got a fuel problem I’ve got to worry about. I have a [command and control] problem I have to worry about when I move around more.”

Spain said Iran’s proven ability to threaten a base means the Air Force is returning to “a time well before 9/11, where we were preparing to fight a peer adversary in an existential way. We see what that looks like through the experience of [Epic Fury].”

Air base defense has long been a complex problem for Air Force leaders. Ostensibly, the Army is responsible for protecting air bases from missile attacks, dating back to the 1948 Key West Agreement on roles and missions of the armed forces. That’s why the Patriot ballistic missile defense system is an Army weapon system. But with the rise of low-cost attack drones such as the Iranian Shahed, the scale and scope of threats has grown while the Army’s capacity to defend far-flung bases has not kept pace. In April 2025, the Air Force published new doctrine on “Point Defense of Air Bases,” assuming a more active role for Airmen in defending their air bases.

The lack of hardened shelters at most forward bases contributes to the Air Force’s vulnerability. Investment in such structures and other passive defenses has often ranked low among budget priorities, compared to aircraft and major research initiatives.

Deptula maintains that the Air Force has long been underfunded and that vulnerabilities are the result of calculated risk and budget choices.

“How come hardened aircraft shelters weren’t in place at Prince Sultan Air Base? How come the command-and-control facility at Al Udeid—that the joint force air component commander has been operating from since 2001—wasn’t built underground?” Deptula said. “The answer is money, because it costs more money. The United States military took the risk, understanding that there were threats out there, they were willing to take the risk and not to spend the money to build hardened aircraft shelters, to build underground facilities.”

Now that “the threat has shown itself to be highly capable,” he added, “resources are going to have to be allocated to increase our ability to defend our bases.”

Air Mobility Command Boss Lt. Gen. Daniel H. Tulley said he was encouraged by Wilsbach’s decision to establish a new career field to develop point defense specialists. Wilsbach said the Air Force will start designating Airmen with the new specialty within two years. The Air Force announced it was standing up the new career field in late June after the Corona meeting. As a short-term fix, USAF has established point defense flights, specialized units of roughly 20 Airmen each, trained to rapidly deploy to hotspots and defend air bases against drone attacks.

Tulley saw how unprotected Al Udeid was when he commanded the 379th Air Expeditionary Wing there from 2019 to 2021.

“When I was at Al Udeid, this problem was widely recognized,” Tulley said. “The Air Force has been going after it, but I think our sense of urgency has dramatically increased—which it needs to. We’ve all seen what Operation Spiderweb did in Russia. How do we prevent the same sort of thing, and maintain the sense of urgency?”

The Air Staff and Point Defense Task Force, working with the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401, or JIATF 401, is making headway to identify technologies and field new weapons to counter the drone threat. But it will take years for the service to build up an adequate point defense capability.

“Would I like to get there a lot faster? Yes, but I think we’re getting there,” Tulley said. “I’d like to look back in two years and say, ‘We’re done,’ but I don’t know if we’ll quite be there yet.”

The Air Force relies primarily on the Small Unmanned Air Defense Systems, or SUADS, for countering drones. The system is capable of identifying and tracking enemy missiles or drones of multiple sizes, and downing incoming drones with an electronic warfare weapon. To stop missiles, it uses both electronic warfare and kinetic effectors. It can also interface with commercial counter-drone systems and other air defense systems, depending on the needs of a commander.

It’s available in two variants, one for fixed air bases and one that can be deployed on a pallet for rapid response missions. The Air Force has requested more than $1.5 billion for SUADS in the fiscal 2027 budget, with most of the funding allocated for the system’s missile defense components, according to budget documents.

What remains unclear is how much money is being spent on additional counter-drone systems for the Air Force, which are being acquired with the assistance of JIATF 401. Those buys are difficult to track since they are not listed in the budget request. Both Air Force and JIATF 401 officials declined to provide funding details.

During the conference, leaders said the Air Force is working on initiatives to gain more oversight over the acquisition process to more efficiently manage its counter-drone acquisitions.

Globally, the market is expanding rapidly, The current global counter-drone market is valued at roughly $9 billion and is projected to reach about $30 billion by 2031.

JIATF-401 Director Army Brig. Gen. Matthew Ross cited that figure in a talk with industry members Sept. 15. The U.S. portion of the counter-drone market is currently valued at roughly $2.5 billion and is expected to grow to roughly $8.6 billion by 2030, according to MarketsandMarkets.com a business intelligence firm.

“What that means is that demand is going up really quickly,” said Ross adding that his agency is acquiring “additional arrows to put into the quiver of our warfighters,” but “our supplies just aren’t there yet.”

Meink said the service is also looking at establishing a senior portfolio acquisition executive, or PAE, to manage the point defense enterprise. PAEs are a new construct, introduced during recent Pentagon acquisition reforms to get more authority into the hands of fewer leaders in order to maximize acquisition success. The idea is to combine several programs within a single mission area and give PAEs authority to move funds between programs and adjust requirements based on evolving needs. The Department of the Air Force currently has 26 PAEs—17 in the Air Force, nine in the Space Force.

Currently, the Air Force PAE for Electronic Systems oversees counter-drone acquisition efforts and the service’s PAE for Intelligence, Surveillance, Reconnaissance & Special Operations Forces manages offensive drone acquisitions, said Lea Kirkwood, the Air Force PAE for Electronic Systems.

The Pentagon recently stood up the new Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems, or DRPM UxS, with the goal of accelerating the development, procurement, and fielding at scale of autonomous capabilities.

“There’s a lot of considerations across mission areas,” Kirkwood said, adding that the Department of the Air Force is “looking at how do we need to look at our structure to say ‘how can we best support the [Pentagon], the DRPM UxS, and then also within the DAF, both from the offensive and the defensive perspective’—you know, what’s the best way to get after this?”

The Air Force is also creating a “point defense weapon system,” Wilsbach said during his speech. The new system will be designed to formally manage multiple counter-drone systems that range from sensors, radars, and command and control architecture to kinetic and nonkinetic effectors for disabling or destroying incoming drones.

“The point defense weapon system is a way for us to consolidate these capabilities under a single umbrella,” Michael Sheehy, director of future operations under the Air Force deputy chief of staff for operations said during the JIATF 401 industry meeting.

The Air Force is currently writing a program action directive for the weapon system. “That way it’s not this ad hoc approach to this, where it is buying some, trying some pieces of parts and then kind of making up who’s operating the system. … The other thing that it does is it creates a single point for funding within the Air Force,” Sheehy added. “Now I have a program element code for this weapon system, and as funding’s coming in, it’s going to that as opposed to kind of going all over the place.”

Sheehy noted that there was a “vast difference” in the amount of counter-drone innovations on the show floor at the AFA conference this year compared to prior shows.

“There’s a lot of counter-UAS capability that is being developed out there, and … we need to have a more enterprise level approach to doing this,” he said. The Air Force “owes it to our wing commanders to provide that kit, provide that training, provide that organization that is professionalized to get after this really difficult problem.”
